_about.what: The numbers of a fleet action fought out on the field (src/battle/sea). Every ship's weight, toughness and nation's quality come from data/campaign/navy.json, as the rules count them: this file only says how the field plays them out. Abstract by design (project memory air-battle-paused, ruling 217): pieces wear each other down within reach, by the angle their guns bear; nothing is aimed and nothing flies.
_about.field: The sea is a square of 'size' metres. The attacker's fleets come on from the south edge, 'edge' metres in, the defender's from the north, in rows 'row' metres apart: destroyers ahead, then cruisers, battleships and carriers. 'limit' is the battle time in seconds before it is called on the exchange so far.
_about.classes: speed in metres a second at cruising speed (the historian's: battleships 11, cruisers 13, destroyers 14, carriers 13); turn in radians a second at full way (a ship turns slower when slow, and barely at all when stopped); reach is the furthest its guns hit at all (the one ring the screens draw) and a ship nearer the enemy than three quarters of best turns away to open the range; per is how many ships of the class sail as one piece (destroyers in fours); crew is a ship's company, for the after-action card only; len and beam are a ship's length and breadth in metres, for the screens and the 3D models; a piece's ships sail in line ahead, three lengths apart. Battleships, cruisers and destroyers have one reach and hit with one punch for each unit of their weight (the design director, b415, upheld by ruling 239): the campaign's card already prices a battleship as more weight than a cruiser, so the field does not count the class a second time. Reach by class was measured and withdrawn: reach is worth weight (the longer reach lands its weight first, and early harm compounds), and the card prices weight, not reach. A destroyer's smaller guns are left to the look. Classes differ in speed, turning, toughness and their place in the line, and their salvos differ in look only (battleships slow and heavy, destroyers quick and light: SALVO in src/battle/ui/sea-draw.ts), with the same harm per unit of weight each minute. A carrier fights by its strike, not its guns: standoff is how far it keeps from the nearest enemy, behind its own screen and beyond the guns' reach.
_about.speeds: Shares of a class's cruising speed for the speed order, and accel, how fast way is gained or lost (metres a second, each second).
_about.fire: rate turns weight into wear on a hull each second, the same for every class. hull: a side's hulls together come to this many times its weight, shared over its ships by the rules' toughness (a battleship takes about twice the wear of its weight that a destroyer does); every shot, strike and raid takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on, so toughness decides which ships go down and not who wins. far is what a piece does at the edge of its reach against 1 at its best range or closer: 1, so guns tell as hard anywhere in reach, and a ship in the rear rows is not worth less than its weight for standing further back (at 0.5, a fleet strong in the ships behind the line won 10 points less than the card). endOn is what its guns do when the target is dead ahead or astern, against 1 on the beam: crossing the T. damaged: a crippled ship still fights at this share. retarget: seconds between a piece looking for a new target.
_about.nerve: A piece's nerve falls by 'hit' for each whole hull it takes in wear, and when a ship of its own side goes down within 'nearR' metres by 'near' times that ship's share of its side's weight (a cruiser lost from a fleet of weight 60 shakes it by 0.06, a destroyer by 0.02, a battleship by 0.2: the design director, b438), so a fleet of many light ships is shaken no more for the same weight lost; out of the fight for 'quiet' seconds it mends at 'mend' a second. Below 'waver' it wavers and fights at 'wavering'; below 'break' it breaks off for its own edge.
_about.side: A side breaks off when it has lost 'breakAt' of its strength as the card counts it, its ships and its coasts' aircraft together (a share of 'spread' either way, more with a good admiral: 'admiral' a level). After a side breaks, its enemy has 'pursuit' seconds to make it pay before the battle ends. The luck of the day is the rules' own: one roll of the dice's run (0.8 to 1.2, navy.ts seaBattles) for the battle, the attacker's ships fighting that much better and the defender's that much worse, so that with nobody playing the field gives what the dice give. Once the enemy has broken off, every ship of the side still fighting runs it down at full speed, the player's as the staff's, until the player gives an order of their own (b402). An order from the chasing side to hold, to break off or to steer for a point lets the beaten enemy go: the action ends there, the side that broke off beaten and the losses as they stand (b458). An order to attack it is a pursuit, and the chase runs on. A ship still afloat at the end with 'hurt' of its hull or less left, or gone out of the fight burning, came home badly hurt: the after card names it by its kind, the enemy's as the player's, so a victory over a fleet that took its wrecks home reads as one (b458).
_about.strike: A carrier's strike: ordered, it is flown within the second and lands 'windup' seconds later on the target and the ships near it within 'radius', and the carrier can strike again 'every' seconds after that. A strike carries the weight of 'every' seconds of the carrier's own weight at 'share', its own weight being what is left of its air group. It takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it falls on (wear in proportion to the ship's hull), so the screen is no cheaper a target than the battleship. Every blow on a side, by gun, strike or raid, wears the whole of what the side brought by weight: the ship it fell on for the gun ships' share, each carrier for its own (as a hull wears, but out of its air group: it stays afloat) and the coasts' aircraft for theirs (b415). Kept whole at 6,000 m while the gun ships wore, carriers were worth more the longer the gun fight ran, a tenth or more of the card either way with the fleets' make-up; worn with their fleet, share 0.34 keeps them within the dice attacking and attacked, with a light screen or a mixed one. Carriers with no gun ship at all are not: the field cannot honour an action where one side has none, so the staff settles it and the field is not offered it (the design director, b438: carriers against carriers is an air battle, and the field flies no planes). With no strike ordered, or under a fleet order, a carrier strikes by its job (jobs.strike): the enemy's carriers first, then battleships, cruisers and destroyers, the one nearest its fleet's main effort; where its style shares fire out (spread), a second carrier takes a second enemy carrier before doubling up. A strike ordered on one piece goes where it is sent. Hit the flight decks first, then the battleships (the panel's principle; Midway, June 1942). Once a side has broken off, no carrier flies a new strike unless the player has sent it after the beaten enemy since (b458): the staff's carriers, and a carrier left to itself, let the enemy go. It is counted, not flown: no aircraft are on the field, and a strike in the air does not slow the screens' fast approach, which runs until the guns meet (b458).
_about.air: Aircraft from the coasts (the rules' airOver, times navy.json air.weight) raid every 'every' seconds, the first within the first raid's span; each raid's weight is 'share' of what that much weight of guns would deal in the time, as a strike's is, and like gunfire it takes the same weight out of the fight whatever ship it finds. A raid finds its ship by the campaign's own aim (carriers.json strike.aim, read only: carriers 3, battleships 2, cruisers 1, destroyers 0.5), times the ships afloat in each piece, with one draw as before. The card counts the coasts' aircraft in a side's strength, so the field does: they are worn by every blow on their side by their share of its weight, and having no hull they lose the whole of it, where a ship's hull takes it at 'fire.hull' (b415). Each raid is as strong as the aircraft left. Share 0.55 keeps the coasts' aircraft within the dice on either side, from a few against a fleet to most of a side's strength. It was 0.5 until every class drew up on one front (b458, see pieces): a gun fleet's whole weight then came to bear, and a fleet of 16 ships won 62 and 65 in 100 at even odds, attacking and attacked, against 8 destroyers whose side was four fifths aircraft. At 0.55 it wins 47 either way, and at 0.6, 31 and 36.
_about.pieces: No more than 'most' pieces a side: past that, cruisers sail in twos, then destroyers in more than fours. Every class's row is 'front' metres times its share of its side's weight, the same metres for every class, with its pieces spaced evenly along it: a row of battleships, carriers, cruisers or destroyers that carries a third of its side's weight is a third of 3,250 m wide. So two fleets of the same weight meet on the same front whatever their make and however many pieces they come in (b438, b458). 'front' replaced 'frontage' (the design director, b458), which spaced each class at its own natural gap (650 m between big ships, 500 m between fours of destroyers, at a side's weight of 50), so that each unit of a side's weight stood on 3,250 m of front in a battleship row, 4,643 m in a carrier row, 6,250 m in a destroyer row and 10,833 m in a cruiser row. A light line then stood two or three times as wide as a battle line of the same weight, its wings out of reach: 12 cruisers and 12 destroyers won 31 in 100 against 3 battleships, 2 cruisers and 8 destroyers at even odds, and 'Carriers against a battle line' won 66 against a card of 71. On one front they win 45 and 70. 3,250 m keeps a battleship row as wide as it was. At 2,500 m the largest fleets fell further from the card, and at 3,600 m or more a fleet of 23 pieces lost 97 in 100 at even odds to one of 18 of much the same make.
_about.ai: The computer's captains (and the player's, where no order is given): each side has a main effort, the enemy piece nearest the middle of its own fleet, kept until it goes or breaks off, when the enemy then nearest the middle that is still fighting takes its place. Around it each ship does its class's job ('jobs'). That is exactly what a newcomer does (select all, right-click the enemy nearest the middle, Space): an order to attack given to two or more pieces is a fleet order, which sets the main effort and leaves each piece to its job, so the newcomer's battle and the staff's are the same (b402, ruling 239). An order to one piece alone is its own target. A ship further than 'keep' metres from the middle of its own fleet works back toward it as it fights. A ship steers for the enemy nearest it, and for the main effort only when that lies more than 'beyond' metres further off than the nearest enemy (ruling 226, 4: every ship sent at one point made a knot the enemy fought around). Until the guns first meet, a fleet keeps together: its gun ships sail at the speed of its slowest gun ship, and one more than 'station' metres ahead of the rearmost of them slows to half that speed until the line comes up, so the screen closes up on the battle line and stays just ahead of it (the historian: fleet speed was the slowest heavy ship's, and the screen kept station on the battle line). Drawn up 700 m a row apart and each at its own speed, a battle line reached the fight a minute after its screen and lost to a light fleet of the same weight 95 times in 100; with the screen kept 600 m ahead it still came 13 in 100 short (b407, ruling 217). A fleet keeps together only to meet a gun line: not once either side has broken off (the chase runs at full speed) and not against an enemy with no gun ship left: then every gun ship not sent at a speed of its own runs the carriers down at full speed, as a broken enemy is. While it keeps together a fleet also holds one course, from its own middle to the enemy's, so the line comes on as it drew up: each steering for the enemy nearest it, the wings turned in toward the middle and the line came on bunched (b438). A ship the player sends at a speed of their own, or on a course, goes as told. A ship within 'broadside' metres of the enemy it is steering for turns to bring its broadside to bear; further off it closes. Closing until 3,450 m left the ships behind their own screen end-on for the whole fight.
_about.evade: A carrier group without battleships that sees an enemy battleship within 'see' metres of a carrier turns away from it and opens the range at 'speed' times a carrier's cruising speed, launching as it goes, unless the player has ordered it to steer, hold or withdraw (a carrier evades even when ordered to strike). Near the edge of the field it turns along it. 'screen' is how near a carrier a ship of its screen must be to turn away with it: 0, so the screen stays and fights (b402: a screen that ran with its carriers left the plain order short of the card). A fleet with battleships of its own stands and fights, its carriers behind the line.
_about.jobs: Each ship class to its own job (the tactics panel's item 2, ruling 239): 'fire' lists, for each gun class, the enemy classes it fires on, in order; 'strike', the enemy classes a carrier strikes, in order (see strike). A piece takes the first class it has in reach, ships still fighting before ships breaking off, and among them the one nearest its fleet's main effort; a style that shares the big guns' fire out ('spread' 1) has each battleship and cruiser take, among them, the one fewest of its side's battleships and cruisers are firing on (ties: nearest the main effort, then its own left), and keep it until another has two fewer. So big guns go on big ships and no enemy big ship is left untroubled, cruisers fight cruisers and back the line, and destroyers fight destroyers and cruisers, turning their guns on battleships and carriers only when nothing else is in reach: a destroyer's shells burst on a big ship's upper works and never pierced its belt (Samar, October 1944; Hiei, November 1942), and its real blow at a big ship is the torpedo run (torp). A bar on destroyer guns firing at big ships was measured and withdrawn (ruling 239): it held priced weight out of the fight. No dice: the same ships in the same places make the same choice. The navies shared fire so that no enemy capital ship went unengaged, and cruisers engaged cruisers (the panel's history notes).
_about.torp: The destroyers' torpedo run (the tactics panel's item 3, ruling 239). A destroyer piece whose guns have nothing in reach banks their weight each second after the guns first meet (fire's rate times its weight, its nerve and the day, with no range or angle), up to 'bank' seconds' worth, and that bank is its salvo: weight its guns could not fire, so the card's weight is moved, not added to. On a run its guns keep firing at whatever their job finds in reach, so a run takes no weight out of the fight. A run: once its side's style allows it (styles: torpWhen), a steady destroyer piece outside the screen goes for the enemy big ship nearest the main effort within 'start' metres, battleships first, then cruisers, then carriers; with spread 1 one run to each target before any second. It closes at flank, launches at its style's 'press' range, turns away at flank for 'away' seconds and rejoins; it may run again 'again' seconds after it launched. Wavering on the run-in breaks it off, its bank kept for the next. The salvo runs 'travel' seconds and falls on its target, as any blow does (the same weight out of the fight whatever it falls on); with the target gone, on the enemy nearest where it was aimed within 'radius' metres, else on the heaviest. The runs open at first contact, or once the enemy's big ships in reach of the side's big guns are shaken to torpWhen of their nerve on average, or 'after' seconds after contact; and at once, whatever the style, for a destroyer piece whose guns have only a battleship or a carrier to fire on, so it is seen closing to launch, not trading shots at full reach. The screen (styles: screen) is the destroyer pieces nearest the side's big ships as it draws up: each keeps 'station' metres ahead of the big ship it guards, toward the enemy, until its guns find a target, and then fights where it is, as the line's other pieces do (held on station, its weight stood out of the fight); it steers for any enemy run within 'intercept' metres and fires first on destroyers making a run; it never runs, and launches its bank from station at an enemy big ship that comes within press. A fleet with no big ship keeps no screen. Once no enemy destroyer is afloat its job is done, and its pieces run and fight as any other destroyer does (the design director, 22:57Z). Destroyers screened the line and attacked in groups with torpedoes, then turned away (North Cape, December 1943; Samar, October 1944: the panel's history notes).
_about.styles: How a side's captains fight (ruling 239): a temperament, not a weapon. The card has priced the fight, so a style changes how the action unfolds, never how much weight each side brings. 'spread': 1 shares the big guns' fire out over the enemy's big ships (jobs), 0 fires on the one nearest the main effort. 'torpWhen': the destroyers' runs open once the enemy big ships in the big guns' reach average this much of their nerve or less (1, at first contact). 'press': the range a run closes to before it launches, in metres. 'screen': the share of the side's destroyer pieces kept back as the screen, rounded down, and at least one where the share is above 0 and there are two or more. 'cover': the share of each carrier strike held back as fighters over the fleet when the enemy brings aircraft (cap); a strike the player orders holds back the same share (ruling 239, 12).
_about.cap: Fighters and guns over the fleet (ruling 239; the tactics panel's item 3, at sea): two neutral trades, so they move where weight falls, never how much. Fighters: when the enemy brings aircraft (a carrier with its air group, or the coasts' aircraft), each carrier flies (1 - cover) of its strike and holds the rest over the fleet, its side's pool; what it holds and has not spent flies with its next strike, so nothing is lost. A strike or a raid of weight W coming in is met by the pool and denied min(pool, W x cap.spoil x the square root of pool / (pool + W)): cap.spoil is the campaign's own (carriers.json cap.spoil, 0.8; air.ts), and the pool pays what it denies, weight for weight, out of each carrier's cover by its share. Guns: the gun ships within the strike's radius of the ship it finds deny f of what is left, f the sum of their ships times carriers.json flak.ships times flak.per, to at most flak.most (0.12), the campaign's own law; each ship pays its share, weight for weight, out of its own next gunfire, and a ship that leaves the fight hands what it owes to the nearest of its side still fighting. Both are told as events, 'sea:cap' (the share the fighters denied) and 'sea:flak' (what the guns denied), for the 3D game: fighters circling over the fleet, flak over the screen.
_about.carrierBattle: Where both sides bring carriers and neither a battleship (ruling 239, 11): 'field' fights it out here, carriers striking from beyond the guns' reach; 'staff' leaves it to the dice, as an action where one side has no gun ship is (b438). It stays 'field' until the design director has read how many such actions the campaign fights.
